subject: Physics
title: Gravitation
summary: Every mass attracts every other mass with F = Gm₁m₂/r². This one law explains falling apples, planetary orbits (Kepler's laws) and satellites.
g = GM/R² at the surface. It decreases with height (1/r²), decreases linearly with depth, and is zero at the centre of the Earth.
Gravitational potential V = −GM/r and potential energy U = −GMm/r are negative: you must supply energy to pull a mass away to infinity.
Orbital speed √(GM/r), escape speed √(2GM/R) and satellite energy E = −GMm/2r are the core results; a satellite's kinetic energy = −(total energy) = −U/2.

formulas.name: Newton's law of gravitation
formulas.formula: F = G m₁ m₂ / r²,   G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²
formulas.when: Force between two point masses (or spheres, centre to centre).
formulas.mistake: r is centre-to-centre distance, not surface-to-surface.

formulas.name: Acceleration due to gravity
formulas.when: Relating g to the planet's mass and radius.

formulas.name: g at height h
formulas.formula: g_h = g R²/(R + h)²   ≈ g(1 − 2h/R) for h ≪ R
formulas.note: Use the exact form when h is comparable to R — the approximation fails.

formulas.name: g at depth d
formulas.note: g is zero at the centre and maximum at the surface.

formulas.name: Effect of rotation (latitude λ)
formulas.when: Weight at the equator vs the poles.
formulas.note: g is least at the equator and greatest at the poles.

formulas.name: Gravitational potential energy
formulas.when: Energy of a mass in a planet's field.
formulas.note: U is negative; near the surface ΔU ≈ mgh only when h ≪ R.

formulas.name: Gravitational potential
formulas.formula: V = −GM/r (outside);  inside a solid sphere V = −GM(3R² − r²)/(2R³)
formulas.when: Work per unit mass to bring a mass from infinity.

formulas.name: Escape speed
formulas.when: Minimum speed to leave the planet for ever.
formulas.mistake: It does not depend on the mass of the body or the direction of throw.

formulas.name: Orbital speed
formulas.formula: v₀ = √(GM/r) = √(gR²/r);  near the surface v₀ = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s
formulas.when: Speed of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r = R + h.

formulas.name: Time period of a satellite
formulas.when: Orbit time; geostationary T = 24 h at h ≈ 36,000 km.

formulas.name: Energy of a satellite
formulas.when: Energy to launch or move a satellite.
formulas.note: Total energy is negative for a bound orbit; binding energy = +GMm/2r.

formulas.name: Kepler's laws
formulas.formula: 1) orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus;  2) equal areas in equal times (dA/dt = L/2m = constant);  3) T² ∝ a³
formulas.note: The second law is conservation of angular momentum — speed is highest at perihelion.

formulas.name: Relation vₑ and v₀
formulas.formula: vₑ = √2 × v₀ (for an orbit at the surface)
formulas.note: A satellite needs ≈41% extra speed to escape.

examples.title: Force between two people
examples.problem: Two 50 kg masses are 1 m apart. Gravitational force?
examples.solution: F = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 50 × 50 / 1² ≈ 1.67 × 10⁻⁷ N — far too small to feel.

examples.title: g at height R/2
examples.problem: Find g at a height R/2 above the Earth (g = 9.8 m/s²).
examples.solution: g_h = g/(1 + 1/2)² = (4/9) × 9.8 ≈ 4.36 m/s². (The approximation g(1 − 2h/R) = 0 would be badly wrong here.)

examples.title: g in a deep mine
examples.problem: g at a depth of 1600 km (R = 6400 km)?

examples.title: Escape speed of Earth
examples.problem: M = 6 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m. Escape speed?

examples.title: Satellite at 360 km
examples.problem: Orbital speed and period at h = 360 km (same M, R)?

examples.title: Kepler's third law
examples.problem: A geostationary satellite (T = 24 h) has orbital radius r. Period at radius r/4?

examples.title: Escape speed of another planet
examples.problem: A planet has twice the Earth's mass and twice its radius. Escape speed? (Earth 11.2 km/s)
examples.solution: vₑ ∝ √(M/R) = √(2/2) = 1 → 11.2 km/s, the same as Earth.

examples.title: Thrown at half the escape speed
examples.problem: A body is thrown up with vₑ/2. Maximum height (R = 6400 km)?
examples.solution: ½m(vₑ/2)² = GMm(1/R − 1/(R+h)) with vₑ² = 2GM/R: GM/4R = GM/R − GM/(R + h) → 1/(R + h) = 3/(4R) → R + h = 4R/3, so h = R/3 ≈ 2133 km.

topics.title: Universal gravitation
topics.explain: Gravity is always attractive, acts along the line joining the masses, follows Newton's third law and works through any medium. It is the weakest fundamental force but dominates at large scales because masses don't cancel like charges.

topics.title: Shell theorem
topics.explain: A uniform spherical shell attracts an outside mass as if all its mass were at the centre, and exerts zero force on a mass inside it. That is why g falls linearly inside a solid sphere.

topics.title: Variation of g
topics.explain: Height: g ∝ 1/r². Depth: g ∝ r (inside). Rotation and the Earth's shape make g smallest at the equator and largest at the poles. A body weighs nothing at the centre of the Earth.

topics.title: Potential and potential energy
topics.explain: Potential is zero at infinity and negative everywhere else. Work done by an external agent = m(V_final − V_initial). For a mass moved from the surface to a height h: ΔU = GMmh/[R(R + h)] = mgh/(1 + h/R).

topics.title: Satellites
topics.explain: A satellite is in free fall around the planet — gravity provides the centripetal force. Orbital speed, period and energy depend only on r, not on the satellite's mass. Astronauts feel weightless because they and the craft fall together.

topics.title: Geostationary and polar satellites
topics.explain: Geostationary: period 24 h, above the equator, moving west to east, height ≈ 36,000 km — used for communication. Polar satellites: low height (~500–800 km), pass over the poles — used for weather and remote sensing.

topics.title: Escape and binding energy
topics.explain: To escape, total energy must be ≥ 0. Energy needed to take a satellite from orbit r to infinity = GMm/2r. Energy to raise a satellite from orbit r₁ to r₂ = GMm/2 (1/r₁ − 1/r₂).

topics.title: Kepler's laws in exams
topics.explain: Areal velocity is constant, so a planet moves fastest at perihelion: v_p r_p = v_a r_a. For ellipses use the semi-major axis a in T² ∝ a³.

ratta: F = Gm₁m₂/r²;  G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
g_h = g(R/(R+h))²;  g_d = g(1 − d/R);  g = 0 at centre.
vₑ = √(2gR) ≈ 11.2 km/s;  v₀ = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s;  vₑ = √2 v₀.
